stimulus:
Shards (use any, ignore the rest, let them collide):

- lichen: two kingdoms sharing one body; the boundary is the organism
- tide-pool desiccation, then sudden return of water
- a cathedral bell whose flaw gives it its pitch
- cuneiform tablets baked accidentally by the fire that destroyed the archive
- ant trail evaporating pheromone: memory that must be forgotten to function
- the sommelier's vocabulary: "flinty," "barnyard," "wet stone"
- error-correcting codes in DNA repair; a typo that is also a signature
- potlatch: status gained by destroying wealth
- moiré: two regular grids producing a pattern neither contains
- the negative space between roots
- a ferry timetable written for passengers who never arrive
- mycelial relay: the slowest network, the longest memory
- kintsugi, but for a broken measurement
- the quiet minute after an earthquake when dogs already knew
- pidgin becoming creole in one generation of children
- a lock that only opens when slightly wrong key is used
- the amateur's blunder that a veteran has trained away
- sandpile avalanches: the same grain, a different cause each time

Instruction to self: before answering, pick two shards that feel least related to the question. Force a structural analogy from each: what is the mechanism, what is inverted, what is being kept because it is flawed, what is being forgotten on purpose? Propose ideas that import those mechanisms, and avoid the first three ideas that come to mind.

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: Pheromone-trail decay: AP-1 occupancy half-life after stimulus withdrawal
ideas.description: Pulse cells with a stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury cytokines, or optogenetic ERK), then track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, chromatin accessibility and enhancer H3K27ac by time-course CUT&Tag/ATAC over days to weeks. Memory is supported if AP-1-marked sites persist well beyond the decay of AP-1 protein and transcription, and the persistence is selective for previously stimulated sites rather than a general slow decay.

ideas.title: Slightly-wrong-key test: dose and dominant-negative titration of AP-1 at the priming and recall steps
ideas.description: Use degron-tagged JUN/FOS or inducible dominant-negative A-FOS (or partial-affinity motif variants) to deplete or weaken AP-1 only during priming, only during the rest period, or only at re-challenge. If AP-1 is needed only at priming to establish the memory but not at recall, it is an initiator, while a requirement at recall means it is a reader. Partial or mismatched motif variants should show whether graded AP-1 input produces graded memory.

ideas.title: Moiré test: combinatorial dimer and cofactor composition of memory sites
ideas.description: Profile which FOS/JUN/ATF dimers and partner factors (e.g., pioneer factors such as BAF or lineage TFs) occupy primed versus naive enhancers using sequential ChIP (re-ChIP) or CUT&RUN with single-molecule footprinting. Test whether memory is carried by the specific combinations that emerge on chromatin after priming, which neither AP-1 nor the partners show alone.

ideas.title: Single-cell lineage-tracked memory inheritance
ideas.description: Combine live reporters of AP-1 activity with barcoded lineage tracing and multiome (scRNA and scATAC) so sister cells can be compared after priming and several divisions. High sister-cell concordance of recall-response magnitude, and of accessibility at AP-1 sites, that exceeds that of unrelated cells would show heritable, cell-autonomous memory, while discordance would indicate transient signaling states.

ideas.title: Sufficiency by site-specific rewriting and erasure
ideas.description: Use dCas9-based tools to deposit or remove AP-1 motifs or AP-1 recruitment at chosen enhancers (e.g., motif deletion by base editing, or dCas9-FOS recruitment) in naive and primed cells. Test whether deleting motifs erases the faster or stronger re-response at that locus, and whether artificially recruiting AP-1 to a naive locus is enough to install a memory-like response without the original stimulus.
